title: Rethinking the Roles of Diffusion and Decoding: Predictive-State Flows for Parallel Language Generation

paper.title: Rethinking the Roles of Diffusion and Decoding: Predictive-State Flows for Parallel Language Generation
paper.abstract:
Abstract In continuous diffusion language models (DLMs), latents generated by the diffusion prior are mapped almost deterministically to tokens, either by a decoder or through a token embedding matrix.
Unlike in image generation, where visual details can vary continuously, the diffusion prior must capture fine-grained discrete token choices in continuous space, which can make the joint latent distribution difficult to model.
We argue that generative roles should instead be divided: the diffusion prior should generate high-level predictive information , while the decoder should resolve the remaining token-level choices.
Based on this view, we introduce Predictive-State Flows (PSF), which partitions a sequence into blocks and associates each block with a predictive state computed solely from the preceding context.
A rectified-flow prior generates the sequence of predictive states, after which a block-causal decoder generates all blocks in parallel, autoregressively only within each block.
This design reduces diffusion from L L token-level states to K ≪ L K\ll L predictive states and reduces token-level sequential depth to L / K L/K .
On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter model with K = 8 K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 using 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token document, compared with 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B with 32 sampling steps.
The corresponding measured operating points yield MAUVE@512 of 0.93 and 0.73, respectively.
Controlled comparisons further show that content states, which additionally encode their own blocks, yield 8–16% higher generative perplexity than predictive states, and that replacing sampled predictive-state trajectories with a shared mean lowers MAUVE@512 by 0.11.
These results suggest that latent design for continuous DLMs should consider not only how compactly text is represented, but also how generative roles are divided between the prior and the decoder.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text by iteratively refining multiple token positions in parallel rather than decoding strictly from left to right ( Li et al., 2022 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Nie et al., 2026 ) . Continuous DLMs perform this refinement over continuous states that are subsequently decoded into text ( Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . In many existing formulations, the generated states are mapped nearly deterministically to tokens ( Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) . This assigns most generative roles to the diffusion prior: it must specify fine-grained token choices, while the decoder largely recovers choices already encoded in those states. This raises a fundamental question: which information should be generated by the diffusion prior, and which decisions should be left to the decoder? This division of roles arises in part from how continuous text representations are commonly learned. An encoder maps an observed token sequence to latents, and a decoder is trained to reconstruct the same sequence ( Lovelace et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Such an objective encourages the latents to preserve the specific token choices that distinguish the observed text from other plausible realizations, leaving the prior responsible for generating those choices. Unlike in image generation, where perceptual compression can discard visually negligible details and represent the remaining variation continuously ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , reconstruction-based text latents tend to preserve fine-grained discrete token distinctions. The diffusion prior must therefore model these distinctions and their dependencies in continuous space, making the joint latent distribution difficult to learn. We therefore propose a different division of generative roles: the diffusion prior generates predictive information that guides subsequent content, while a decoder resolves the remaining local token choices. We instantiate this principle using predictive states . Given a sequence x 1 : L ∈ 𝒱 L x_{1:L}\in\mathcal{V}^{L} divided into K K consecutive blocks, we associate each block k k with a continuous state 𝒔 k = E ψ ​ ( x ( < k ) ) , {\bm{s}}_{k}=E_{\psi}\left(x^{(<k)}\right), (1) which summarizes the context preceding block k k without observing the block itself. The state therefore provides information for predicting the upcoming block, rather than directly encoding its specific token choices. We use a rectified-flow prior ( Liu et al., 2022 ) to generate the predictive-state trajectory 𝒔 1 : K {\bm{s}}_{1:K} . Conditioned on these states, a block-causal decoder predicts all K K blocks in parallel, with autoregressive decoding restricted to within each block. We call the resulting framework Predictive-State Flow (PSF). However, this division of roles introduces a consistency challenge. Because the full predictive-state trajectory is generated before token decoding, independently decoded blocks may become inconsistent at their boundaries. We coordinate adjacent blocks through a one-token landing target : after the first parallel decoding step, block k k can condition on the first generated token of block k + 1 k+1 , providing a lightweight constraint on their transition. We further adapt the decoder to rollout states produced by the learned prior, reducing the train–generation mismatch. This division also supports parallel generation: the prior operates on K ≪ L K\ll L predictive states, while the decoder generates the corresponding blocks concurrently. With autoregression restricted to within each block, the decoder requires only L / K L/K sequential token-generation steps instead of L L . Our experiments directly evaluate this division of generative roles. On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter PSF model with K = 8 K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 while requiring only 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token sequence, compared with 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B. In a controlled comparison, content states that also encode their own block are 8–16% worse than predictive states. Under nucleus sampling, PSF achieves a generative perplexity of 19.4 when the prior generates only predictive states, compared with 21.2 when it additionally generates latent variables carrying information about each block’s token realization. This supports leaving local token choices to the decoder at long block lengths. Further reducing K K from 64 to 8 also improves perplexity from 39.2 to 22.8 while lowering the computational cost of the diffusion prior. This reflect a trade-off between the latent-generation difficulty and the amount of local autoregressive realization. Same-hardware measurements further show that lower FLOPs do not translate directly into wall-clock speedups, as latency and throughput vary with both block length and batch size. Our contributions are summarized as follows. First, we introduce predictive states , which allow the diffusion prior to model high-level predictive information while leaving token-level realization to the decoder. Second, we develop PSF, which generates a short predictive-state trajectory with rectified flow and decodes the corresponding blocks in parallel, using one-token landing targets to coordinate adjacent blocks and local autoregression within each block to limit sequential decoding depth. Third, we empirically study this division of generative roles, showing that predictive states outperform content states and that strong generation quality at long block lengths can be achieved without requiring the prior to encode block-specific token information.

sections.heading: 2 Predictive-State Flow
sections.text: We begin by separating the generation of predictive information from token-level realization. PSF uses a rectified-flow prior to generate a trajectory of predictive states , while a predictive block decoder generates the corresponding token-level realizations. Each predictive state summarizes the context preceding a block without encoding the block itself, allowing the prior to model predictive information while leaving local token choices to the block decoder. The block decoder realizes all blocks in parallel, while a one-token landing target couples adjacent branches to improve consistency across block boundaries.

sections.heading: 2.1 Predictive States
sections.text: We divide a sequence x 1 : L ∈ 𝒱 L x_{1:L}\in\mathcal{V}^{L} into K K consecutive blocks x ( 1 ) , … , x ( K ) x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(K)} of length ℓ = L / K \ell=L/K and associate each block k k with a predictive state 𝒔 k ∈ ℝ d {\bm{s}}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that summarizes the context preceding that block. To ensure that each state contains only information available from the corresponding prefix, we use a block-causal encoder in which representations in block j j depend only on tokens in blocks 1 , … , j 1,\dots,j . We mean-pool the outputs of block j j to obtain a context state 𝒄 j = f ψ ​ ( x ( ≤ j ) ) . {\bm{c}}_{j}=f_{\psi}\!\left(x^{(\leq j)}\right). (2) We then shift these states by one block so that the state associated with block k k depends only on its preceding context: 𝒔 1 = 𝒔 bos , 𝒔 k = 𝒄 k − 1 = f ψ ( x ( < k ) ) , k = 2 , … , K , {\bm{s}}_{1}={\bm{s}}_{\mathrm{bos}},\qquad{\bm{s}}_{k}={\bm{c}}_{k-1}=f_{\psi}\!\left(x^{(<k)}\right),\quad k=2,\dots,K, (3) where 𝒔 bos {\bm{s}}_{\mathrm{bos}} is a learned state representing the empty prefix. By construction, 𝒔 k {\bm{s}}_{k} depends only on x ( < k ) x^{(<k)} , unlike content latents that encode a particular realization of their own block ( Lovelace et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . We refer to the predictive-state trajectory 𝐒 = ( 𝒔 1 , … , 𝒔 K ) \mathbf{S}=({\bm{s}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{s}}_{K}) , optionally together with the realization codes introduced in Section 2.4 , as the document plan . The diffusion prior models this plan, while the block decoder resolves the token-level realization of each block.

sections.heading: 2.2 Parallel Block Decoder with Landing Targets
sections.text: Given the predictive states, the block decoder generates the K K blocks in parallel, with causal self-attention within each block. Block k k cross-attends to 𝒔 ≤ k {\bm{s}}_{\leq k} under a causal mask over the block index. Because predictive states do not specify a unique local realization, independently generated blocks can each be plausible while remaining inconsistent across block boundaries. We address this issue with a one-token landing target . The first decoding step generates the first token of every block in parallel. From the second step onward, block k k additionally conditions on the first token of block k + 1 k+1 . During training, this target is the ground-truth token, whereas during generation it is the token produced at the first decoding step. Let τ k = x 1 ( k + 1 ) \tau_{k}=x^{(k+1)}_{1} for k < K k<K , and let τ K \tau_{K} denote the learned “no-target” embedding supplied to the final block. The block decoder factorizes as p θ ( x ( 1 : K ) ∣ 𝒔 1 : K ) = ∏ k = 1 K [ p θ ( x 1 ( k ) ∣ 𝒔 ≤ k ) ∏ i = 2 ℓ p θ ( x i ( k ) ∣ x < i ( k ) , 𝒔 ≤ k , τ k ) ] . p_{\theta}\!\left(x^{(1:K)}\mid\bm{s}_{1:K}\right)=\prod_{k=1}^{K}\left[p_{\theta}\!\left(x^{(k)}_{1}\mid\bm{s}_{\leq k}\right)\prod_{i=2}^{\ell}p_{\theta}\!\left(x^{(k)}_{i}\mid x^{(k)}_{<i},\bm{s}_{\leq k},\tau_{k}\right)\right]. (4) After the first decoding step, all landing targets are available, and the K K branches proceed in parallel for the remaining steps. The decoder therefore requires only ℓ \ell sequential token-generation steps, rather than L L for standard autoregressive decoding.

We use an x x -prediction parameterization, where the prior predicts the clean trajectory 𝐒 ^ ϕ ​ ( 𝐒 t , t ) \hat{\mathbf{S}}_{\phi}(\mathbf{S}_{t},t) . sections.heading: 2.4 Training
sections.text: Training of PSF proceeds in three stages. We first jointly train the encoder and block decoder for reconstruction. We then freeze the encoder trunk and fine-tune the decoder to improve robustness to generated predictive states, introduce block-specific realization codes, and adapt the model across different block lengths. Finally, we freeze the encoder and decoder and train the flow prior over the resulting plans. Model-specific training schedules and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix A.2 . Stage I: reconstruction training. We first jointly train the encoder and block decoder using token-level cross-entropy, adding Gaussian noise to the predictive states read by the decoder. For block k k , the decoder conditions on the predictive states 𝒔 ≤ k {\bm{s}}_{\leq k} , which summarize only the preceding blocks. Stage II: decoder fine-tuning. We next freeze the encoder trunk and further train the block decoder in three steps: adapting it to rollout states, introducing block-specific realization codes, and adapting it across different block lengths. Training on generated states. During initial training, the block decoder conditions on predictive states encoded from ground-truth sequences. At generation time, however, it conditions on states produced by the flow prior rather than states directly encoded from ground-truth text. To reduce this mismatch, we generate a no-gradient rollout conditioned on the ground-truth predictive states and re-encode the resulting sequence. For each block independently, we replace the original predictive state with its re-encoded counterpart with probability 0.5 0.5 , while keeping the original token targets unchanged. The rollout uses temperature 0.65 0.65 and nucleus sampling with p = 0.95 p=0.95 . We provide a binary source label λ k \lambda_{k} for each predictive state, where λ k = 1 \lambda_{k}=1 denotes an original encoder state and λ k = 0 \lambda_{k}=0 denotes a rollout state. A zero-initialized embedding of λ k \lambda_{k} is added to 𝒔 k {\bm{s}}_{k} . At generation time, we set λ k = 0 \lambda_{k}=0 for all blocks. Realization codes. The predictive state 𝒔 k = 𝒄 k − 1 {\bm{s}}_{k}={\bm{c}}_{k-1} is computed before block k k is observed and therefore contains only information from the preceding blocks. We next augment the decoder with a low-dimensional realization code 𝒓 k ∈ ℝ 64 {\bm{r}}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{64} from the unshifted encoder state 𝒄 k = f ψ ​ ( x ( ≤ k ) ) {\bm{c}}_{k}=f_{\psi}(x^{(\leq k)}) , which additionally contains information from block k k . A newly added linear head predicts the mean and diagonal variance of a Gaussian posterior, q ψ ​ ( 𝒓 k ∣ 𝒄 k ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝁 ψ ​ ( 𝒄 k ) , diag ⁡ ( 𝝈 ψ 2 ​ ( 𝒄 k ) ) ) . q_{\psi}({\bm{r}}_{k}\mid{\bm{c}}_{k})=\mathcal{N}\!\left({\bm{\mu}}_{\psi}({\bm{c}}_{k}),\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\bm{\sigma}_{\psi}^{2}({\bm{c}}_{k})\right)\right). (7) The block decoder conditions on both 𝒓 k {\bm{r}}_{k} and the next-block code 𝒓 k + 1 {\bm{r}}_{k+1} , sampled from their posteriors during training. During this stage, the encoder trunk remains frozen, while the decoder, code head, and newly introduced code-conditioning layers are trained jointly. We regularize the posterior toward 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}) with a KL budget of ℓ \ell nats per block that limits the amount of block-specific information carried by 𝒓 k {\bm{r}}_{k} . Further details of the posterior and conditioning architecture are provided in Appendix A.2 . Training across block lengths. Starting from K = 64 K=64 , we successively fine-tune the decoder at K = 32 K=32 , 16 16 , and 8 8 , while keeping the encoder trunk frozen. Stage III: flow-prior training. Finally, we freeze the encoder and block decoder and train the flow prior described in Section 2.3 . For each training sequence, we encode the predictive states 𝒔 k {\bm{s}}_{k} and use the posterior mean 𝝁 k {\bm{\mu}}_{k} as the target realization code. The prior is trained to jointly generate these representations using the flow-matching objective defined in the previous section. We train a separate prior for each value of K K , warm-started from the previous block length. For K = 8 K=8 , we additionally train a states-only prior that generates only the predictive states, using zero code targets. We retain the code-trained block decoder and fix all its realization-code inputs to 𝟎 \mathbf{0} . At inference time, we use generated codes for K ≥ 16 K\geq 16 and the states-only prior for K = 8 K=8 (Section 3.4 ).

sections.heading: 2.5 Generation and Refinement
sections.text: For generation, we first sample the predictive-state trajectory from the flow prior, together with realization codes when they are used. The block decoder then generates all K K blocks in parallel over ℓ = L / K \ell=L/K autoregressive steps. The first decoding step produces the landing targets, after which each branch conditions on the first token of the following block and continues independently. We set λ k = 0 \lambda_{k}=0 for all blocks during generation. The resulting serial depth is 50 + ℓ 50+\ell , compared with L L steps for standard autoregressive generation. Optionally, we refine the generated document by re-encoding it and running the block decoder again. When realization codes are used, they are recomputed from the re-encoded sequence. Because refinement conditions on encoder-produced states, we set λ k = 1 \lambda_{k}=1 . Each refinement round requires one encoder pass followed by another ℓ \ell -step parallel decode.

sections.heading: 3.1 Main results
sections.text: PSF achieves lower generative perplexity than 32-step ELF-B at matched entropy: at 5.16, the K = 8 K{=}8 states-only configuration with the 4-gram ban reaches 19.0, versus 24.0 for ELF-B (Figure 2 (a)). The plain sampler reaches 22.8; states-only sampling without the ban reaches 19.4 (Figure 3 (a); Appendix B.2 ). PSF-L with the ban reaches 16.4, near the unbanned same-data AR’s 16.0 (Appendix A.6 ). Perplexity falls as K K decreases (Table 1 ; Section 3.3 ). Beyond perplexity, the plain K = 8 K{=}8 sampler reaches MAUVE@512 of 0.93 versus 0.73 for 32-step ELF-B, with comparable cross-sample diversity (Appendices D.2 and D.3 ). The states-only configuration lowers perplexity further, while the plain sampler retains greater distributional similarity and diversity. PSF retains a 7–23% perplexity advantage over BD3-LM on a length-controlled window (Appendix D.2 ). At matched entropy, the best BD3-LM (blocks of 4) is at about twice our perplexity, partly because of its shorter documents. Two Qwen2.5 judges keep the order of the K ≤ 16 K{\leq}16 models relative to 32-step ELF-B and BD3-LM (Appendix D.1 ), and a document-wide 4-gram ban reduces the loop rate to zero at similar matched-entropy perplexity (Appendix D.4 ). Document coherence is evaluated separately (Appendix D.6 ).

Block length and scale. Longer blocks lower generative perplexity and prior cost along the training chain: reducing K K from 64 to 8 lowers perplexity from 39.2 to 22.8 and the prior’s cost from 631 to 138 GFLOPs, whereas BD3-LM degrades as its blocks grow (Figure 4 ). The decoder’s held-out cross-entropy rises from 2.63 to 2.97 nats per token (Appendix B.3 ): predicting a given document and generating text need not improve together. This is consistent with fewer seams and longer within-block context benefiting generation despite coarser states. The larger model helps most with long blocks. We use K = 8 K{=}8 , accepting greater serial depth; the chain does not isolate block length at equal training budget. Training and sampling settings. Training on generated prefixes with source labels brings sampled-plan perplexity close to true-plan decoding (Appendix B.1 ). Using 32 or 64 rather than 50 prior steps changes K = 8 K{=}8 headline perplexities by about 1% (Appendix B.4 ). Results are one-shot: refinement provides no consistent gain at matched entropy (Appendix B.4 ).

sections.heading: 3.4 Predictive states and local realization
sections.text: Predictive against content states. Predictive states yield lower generative perplexity than content states at matched entropy and K = 8 K{=}8 . The content-state control is 8–16% worse across sampling settings and 12% worse in true-plan decode, with a similar plain-sampler loop rate (Table 4 ; Appendix B.2 ). For this control, we replace the predictive state 𝒔 k = 𝒄 k − 1 {\bm{s}}_{k}={\bm{c}}_{k-1} by the content state 𝒄 k = f ψ ​ ( x ( ≤ k ) ) {\bm{c}}_{k}=f_{\psi}(x^{(\leq k)}) , which also encodes its own block, and repeat the final decoder fine-tuning and prior training at the same budget. The gap persists when the prior is bypassed, suggesting that the benefit depends partly on how the decoder uses the representation. Both variants inherit a predictive-state checkpoint, so the result supports this division of work under the shared adaptation protocol. Realization codes and the states-only prior. At matched entropy, generated realization codes lower generative perplexity at the tested K ≥ 16 K{\geq}16 settings but raise it at K = 8 K{=}8 . With code-trained decoders, zeroing the codes raises perplexity by 5–38% at K ≥ 16 K{\geq}16 , but lowers it by 6% (plain) and 9% (nucleus) at K = 8 K{=}8 (Appendix B.2 ). A states-only prior retains the latter gains (Appendix B.2 ). Longer blocks provide more local history, consistent with leaving more realization to the decoder. We therefore generate codes at K ≥ 16 K{\geq}16 and use states-only generation at K = 8 K{=}8 . What the sampled plan controls. Sampled plans yield higher MAUVE@512 than a shared mean plan at K = 8 K{=}8 : 0.866 versus 0.754 at a fixed sampler setting (Appendix B.2 ). Replacing sampled plans by their position-wise mean, with zero codes and fixed decoder noise, also raises PSF’s perplexity by 7–9% and the lexical topic-switch rate from 12–14% to 30–47%. Perplexity is compared at fixed sampler settings; lexical topic-switch rates are interpolated to entropy 5.16. The intervention also changes length and entropy. Re-encoded outputs are closer to their own sampled plan than to another document’s in 98% of cases. These probes support the plan’s role in organizing content; similar sampled-plan and true-plan perplexities alone would not establish that role. Quality of the best configuration. Our lowest-perplexity configuration in Table 1 , PSF-L with the states-only prior, still has a higher lexical topic-switch rate than real text: 9.6% versus 3.6%. Appendices D.5 and D.6 report topic-persistence and LLM-judged coherence evaluations.

sections.heading: 4 Background and Related Work
sections.text: Diffusion and flow models for text. Discrete DLMs corrupt tokens with multinomial or masking noise and learn to reverse it ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2023 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) ; continuous DLMs embed tokens and denoise the embeddings ( Li et al., 2022 ; Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ) . ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) keeps the sequence in a frozen T5 embedding space and reaches a generative perplexity of 24 on OpenWebText in 32 steps; our prior borrows its self-conditioning ( Chen et al., 2022 ) and guidance-scale tokens ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . All of these models denoise the full L L -token sequence at every step; our prior denoises K ≪ L K\ll L latents, and tokens are produced by a separate block decoder. Block-wise and semi-autoregressive generation. BD3-LM ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) , SSD-LM ( Han et al., 2023 ) and AR-Diffusion ( Wu et al., 2023 ) are autoregressive across blocks and diffuse within each block; BD3-LM’s quality degrades as the block grows (Section 3.3 ). Our model is the transpose—diffusion across blocks, autoregression within—so the two families live on one axis, the block length, and we report both ends of it under one ruler. Blockwise parallel, multi-head and speculative decoding ( Stern et al., 2018 ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Leviathan et al., 2023 ) propose tokens and verify them with an autoregressive model; our blocks need no verification step: there is no separate target model to match, and the plan and the landing token are the only cross-block inputs. Planning and hierarchical generation. Plan-and-Write ( Yao et al., 2019 ) uses explicit keyword storylines to guide story generation, while Skeleton-of-Thought ( Ning et al., 2024 ) expands a prompted textual outline in parallel. The Latent Transformer ( Kaiser et al., 2018 ) autoregressively generates a shorter sequence of discrete latents and decodes the target translation in parallel. Our flow prior generates continuous predictive states jointly, and the block decoder realizes tokens autoregressively within each block. Latent diffusion for text. LD4LG ( Lovelace et al., 2023 ) and PLANNER ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) run diffusion in a learned latent space of a sentence or paragraph and decode it autoregressively; Large Concept Models ( Barrault et al., 2024 ) generate sentence embeddings and decode each into its sentence. These representations encode the content to be generated. We generate a sequence of predictive states that exclude their own block, predict the blocks in parallel , and couple adjacent blocks with a one-token landing target.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: This work revisits what a diffusion prior should generate in a continuous diffusion language model. Rather than requiring continuous states to specify the final token sequence, PSF assigns different generative roles to the prior and the decoder: the flow prior generates a short trajectory of predictive states that describe what should come next, while a block decoder resolves the corresponding token-level realizations. One-token landing targets provide lightweight coupling between blocks while preserving parallel block generation. This division of roles yields both computational and modeling benefits. With only K = 8 K=8 predictive states for a 1024-token document, PSF uses 23 × \times fewer FLOPs than 32-step ELF-B while achieving lower generative perplexity, higher MAUVE, and higher batched throughput. When the prior generates predictive states alone, nucleus sampling further reduces matched-entropy perplexity to approximately 20% below ELF-B. More importantly, predictive states consistently outperform content states that additionally encode their own blocks, and increasing block length improves PSF even as it degrades block diffusion. Together, these results suggest that continuous language-model latents should be designed not only for what they represent, but also for how generative roles are divided between the prior and the decoder. A useful latent need not preserve every detail of the output; it can instead represent information that is easy for a continuous prior to generate and sufficient for a decoder to turn into coherent text. Predictive states provide one realization of this principle, and point toward continuous generative models in which priors and decoders are designed jointly around the information each is best suited to generate. Limitations and future work. Our main limitation is scale: all experiments use at most 677M generation parameters, a fixed 1024-token canvas and unconditional OpenWebText generation; larger models and longer sequences remain unexplored. Blocks are decoded in parallel from a shared plan, coupled only by one-token landing targets, so whether many blocks stay consistent in topic, entities and discourse over longer documents is untested; topic persistence is already the weakest aspect of our samples (Appendix D.5 ). The most pressing next steps are to scale model size and sequence length, to couple blocks more strongly than through a single token, and to measure long-range coherence, which generative perplexity misses. Prompted continuation works without retraining but uses the prompt weakly, calling for a prompt-conditioned prior. Autoregressive models remain ahead, although the gap to the same-data baseline narrows at our largest scale (Appendix A.6 ), and the states-only configuration trades topic persistence, diversity and judged coherence for lower perplexity. The FLOP saving over ELF becomes a throughput advantage only at large batch, and the training recipe has several stages, including realization codes whose benefit we only partly understand; faster small-batch sampling and a simpler recipe remain future work.

sections.heading: Compute and software.
sections.text: All training ran on eight H100 80GB GPUs in PyTorch with bfloat16 autocast. Step cost is dominated by the self-realized-prefix rollouts. The timed stages are: PSF’s chain stage at K = 8 K{=}8 , 6.6 s per step (11 hours for 6k steps); for PSF-L, the realization-code stage 1.1 s per step (3.1 hours for 10k steps), the chain stages at K = 32 K{=}32 , 16 16 and 8 8 1.7, 3.0 and 5.6 s per step (3.9, 5.0 and 9.4 hours for 8k, 6k and 6k steps), and a 30k-step prior stage 0.21 s per step (1.8 hours). The remaining stages of Table 6 were not timed. Every inference timing uses one otherwise idle H100 (Appendix C ).

sections.heading: A.3 Evaluation protocol
sections.text: The following protocol defines the quality columns of Table 1 and the interpolated comparisons. Text processing and held-out data. We detokenize each generated document with its native tokenizer (T5, google-t5/t5-small , V = 32,100 V=32{,}100 for PSF and ELF), cut at the first end-of-text token, and re-tokenize with openai-community/gpt2-large . Scoring uses at most the first 1024 judge tokens per document. A fixed random subset of 10,000 OpenWebText documents (split seed 0) is held out from training. Evaluation dumps and the appendix’s held-out rows each contain 1000 documents. Perplexity, entropy and repetition. Generative perplexity is the exponential of the corpus-level mean token negative log-likelihood. Entropy is the unigram entropy of the judge’s tokens, computed per document and averaged in nats; on ELF’s samples our implementation and ELF’s agree to the third decimal. Loop rate is the fraction of documents whose first 256 T5 tokens contain an 8-gram occurring at least three times. MAUVE. MAUVE ( Pillutla et al., 2021 ) compares 1000 generated and 1000 held-out documents using GPT-2 Large’s final-layer state at the last token, with k k -means quantization and five quantization seeds averaged. This feature is sensitive to whether a document ends naturally or is cut at the canvas. Systems that never emit end-of-text (ELF and GPT-2 small at a fixed 1024 tokens) score 0.02–0.46 with the full 1024-token window, reflecting a length artefact (Appendix D.2 ). We therefore restrict both sides to their first 512 judge tokens by default. Cosmos uses 256 on both sides (Appendix A.4 ); scores from different windows are not directly comparable. Interpolation. We obtain “@5.16” values by log-linear interpolation to entropy 5.16, the rounded entropy of ELF-B’s 32-step samples (5.158), with any extrapolations explicitly marked. Perplexity–entropy slopes are 2.2–2.5 log-perplexity units per nat for our models: about 25% higher perplexity per 0.1 nat ( e 0.22 ≈ 1.25 e^{0.22}\approx 1.25 ). The slopes are about 3.4 for ELF-B (Table 8 ) and 5–9 for BD3-LM (Table 7 ), making the choice of bracket especially consequential for BD3-LM. Appendix A.7 lists the brackets and distinguishes measured from interpolated points. Other judges and diagnostics. Appendix D.1 uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen/Qwen2.5-7B under the same protocol, with entropy in Qwen tokens. True-plan decode replaces the sampled plan by the encoder’s plan of a held-out document, assessing the decoder with the prior bypassed. Size in Table 1 counts generation parameters (decoder plus prior; ELF excludes T5).

sections.heading: Cosmos.
sections.text: Cosmos ( Meshchaninov et al., 2026 ) learns smooth BERT representations and reconstructs tokens in parallel. We evaluate its longest released OpenWebText checkpoint at its native 512 BERT tokens and 512 latents, without latent compression. Sampling uses 200 Euler SDE steps with the tan schedule ( d = 5 d{=}5 ), EMA weights, self-conditioning and a parallel greedy decoder: 279M generation parameters and 26.7 TFLOPs per native-length document. Denoising is FP32, with bfloat16 decoder autocast. We sample 1000 documents (500 each at seeds 42 and 43, batch 32), truncate at the first SEP token, and apply the common GPT-2 Large judge, obtaining Gen. PPL 90.65 and entropy 4.760. MAUVE uses the first 256 judge tokens of both generated texts and the same 1000 held-out references: MAUVE@256 is 0.677 ± 0.034 0.677\pm 0.034 over five quantization seeds. Generation remains at the native length. Eager sampling takes 669.7 ms per document, averaged over 28 full batches from two independent single-H100 runs, excluding each warmup and final partial batch. We report this checkpoint only in the appendix because its tokenizer, training preprocessing and native length differ from the 1024-token setup. Its compute is for 512 BERT tokens, and its MAUVE@256 is not directly comparable to the main table’s MAUVE@512.

sections.text: Figure 3 (b) separates retraining without the target from switching it off at inference, which replaces it by the trained “no target” vector at every position, as for the last block. Its K = 64 K{=}64 checkpoint pair is the final-model removal in Table 11 . It uses a uniform-time prior; the logit-normal prior in Table 13 lowers perplexity by 5–6%, explaining why the figure’s curves lie above that table’s K = 64 K{=}64 value. Without the target, K = 64 K{=}64 documents are also shorter. Their lower per-document entropy under the 1024-token protocol can contribute to the matched-entropy gap (Appendix D.2 ). Table 3 instead compares positions at a fixed setting, averaging blocks 2–64 of 500 documents at t = 0.65 t{=}0.65 and nucleus 0.95, without this entropy-matching effect. At K = 8 K{=}8 the lengths are nearly equal. Appendix A.7 records the extended curve settings. At K = 8 K{=}8 , switching off the target gives 23.3 against 22.5 with the nearest brackets as plotted ( + 3.3 % +3.3\% ; + 3.2 % +3.2\% with the 0.70/0.80 pairs on both sides). Retraining gives 23.9 / 22.2 with the plain / nucleus sampler: the figure’s like-for-like gaps are + 6.2 % +6.2\% / + 4.7 % +4.7\% , or + 5.2 % +5.2\% for plain with the 0.70/0.80 pairs. Table 12 reports + 4.8 % +4.8\% for plain against its standard 22.8 baseline, rather than the figure’s 22.5 (Appendix A.7 ). The unplotted inference intervention on PSF-L gives 19.2 against 18.4 ( + 4.5 % +4.5\% ).

sections.heading: The seam with the target.
sections.text: Even with the landing target, the seams remain the most expensive positions. At K = 8 K{=}8 (entropy 5.16; blocks 2 to K K of 500 documents) the judge’s perplexity at the first token of a block is 332 against 18 in mid-block, and rises again to 200 at the last position, where the block lands on the next block’s first token; at K = 16 K{=}16 (entropy 5.11) the first token costs 145 against 17. Halving K K makes boundaries less frequent, consistent with fewer, longer blocks helping generation (Section 3.3 ).

sections.heading: Lookahead and source labels at inference.
sections.text: On the final K = 8 K{=}8 models, zeroing the lookahead code 𝒓 k + 1 {\bm{r}}_{k+1} gives 22.4 against 22.8, and setting the source label to “original state” ( λ k = 1 \lambda_{k}{=}1 ) gives 24.3 against 24.7 at entropy 5.191, but the loop rate rises to 9.3% and 9.9% (against 6.9% and 9%); for PSF-L the lookahead gives 17.2 against 17.1 at entropy 5.130. Perplexity changes little in these inference checks, even where looping increases. Together with the training ablations, they support retaining the landing target, lookahead code and source label at their trained settings by default.

sections.heading: Codes at inference.
sections.text: At K = 8 K{=}8 , the prior’s codes do not improve generative perplexity at matched entropy: shuffling has little effect, and zero codes are 6% (plain) to 9% (nucleus) better, with higher loop rates. Fresh 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) codes are 13% better but raise looping to 19.3%, while scaling codes by 1.5 is 10% worse. The sign reverses with shorter blocks: zeroing codes costs 38%, 22% and 5% at K = 64 K{=}64 , 32 and 16. Under teacher forcing, posterior-mean codes lower decoder NLL at every block length, by 0.94, 0.91, 0.77 and 0.53 nats per token at K = 64 K{=}64 , 32, 16 and 8 (PSF-L: 1.14, 1.08, 0.91 and 0.57). Codes inferred by the prior for the true states recover 80–90% of this gain. The code is a linear read-out of the next predictive state with a budget of about one nat per token; its decreasing NLL benefit is consistent with longer blocks providing more local history. In generation, codes reduce entropy along with perplexity at a fixed temperature, so that benefit need not persist at matched entropy. The K = 8 K{=}8 reversal is also present with true plans: zero instead of true codes gives 19.9 against 24.5 at entropy 5.168 ( − 19 % -19\% ), so it cannot be explained solely by prior prediction errors. The prior’s codes have similar marginal scales to the encoder’s posterior means (standard deviation 1.44 against 1.59 per dimension, norm 11.7 against 13.1). The perplexity gain also has a cost in the paired generation probes. On the same sampled plans at K = 8 K{=}8 , zero codes lower perplexity by 6.3% (plain) and 9.7% (nucleus) at matched entropy, but MAUVE@512 falls by 0.052 / 0.051 and the lexical topic-switch rate rises from 6.9% to 11.8% and from 6.8% to 13.1%. Thus the lowest-perplexity choice need not best preserve the sample distribution or topic persistence.

sections.heading: Retraining and the states-only prior.
sections.text: A decoder retrained without the code channel reaches the zero-code generation numbers in Figure 10 , but its true-plan decode is 18% worse than the code-trained decoder’s with zero codes (21.4 against 18.1 at entropy 5.13). This supports a training benefit under the shared adaptation protocol, despite the inference-time perplexity result. We retain that code-trained decoder and train a states-only prior with zero code targets, continuing the K = 8 K{=}8 prior for 30k steps. Its generated codes come out at zero and it reproduces the zero-code numbers for both sizes without changing the architecture. It supplies the K = 8 K{=}8 states-only rows of Table 1 ; at K ≥ 16 K\geq 16 we retain generated codes.

sections.heading: Predictive against content states.
sections.text: The same adaptation recipe tests whether a block should read a state of its prefix or of the block itself. The control replaces the predictive state 𝒔 k = 𝒄 k − 1 {\bm{s}}_{k}={\bm{c}}_{k-1} by the inclusive state 𝒄 k = f ψ ​ ( x ( ≤ k ) ) {\bm{c}}_{k}=f_{\psi}(x^{(\leq k)}) , a content latent as in segment-level latent diffusion. It retains the frozen encoder trunk, code channel, 6k self-realized-prefix steps from the K = 16 K{=}16 checkpoint and 30k prior steps. Both variants inherit a decoder trained on predictive states, so this tests the indexing choice under shared adaptation, with an initialization that may favor predictive states. The content control has 8–16% higher perplexity across sampling settings and 12% higher true-plan perplexity (Tables 4 and 12 ). The latter gap persists when prior sampling is bypassed, suggesting that it depends partly on how the decoder uses the representation. Loop rates do not follow the same ordering: they are similar with the plain sampler (7.3% against 6.9% at t = 0.75 t{=}0.75 ), and lower for content with zero codes (7.5% / 5.0% against 9.7% / 7.7%). The 4-gram ban changes matched-entropy perplexity by only − 2 % -2\% to + 1 % +1\% (Appendix D.4 ). Two content readings require small extrapolations: 0.015 nats for zero codes with plain sampling and 0.025 nats for true-plan decode.

sections.heading: What the sampled plan controls.
sections.text: Four probes on PSF at K = 8 K{=}8 (1000 documents each; the second also on PSF-L) examine plan use in prediction, generation and representation space. First, under teacher forcing, replacing a document’s predictive states by another document’s, by the dataset-mean state or by its own states with blocks 2–8 permuted costs + 8.0 % +8.0\% , + 7.1 % +7.1\% and + 2.6 % +2.6\% in NLL ( + 9.5 % +9.5\% , + 5.4 % +5.4\% and + 1.8 % +1.8\% with zero codes). The generation probe replaces sampled plans by their position-wise mean, with zero codes and the same block-decoder noise. At fixed sampler settings, this raises perplexity by 7.0–8.7% for PSF (plain, nucleus, states-only, states-only with the ban), and for PSF-L by 7.4–9.6% with nucleus sampling and 0.7–1.5% with the ban. We use fixed settings for this comparison because the intervention also changes length and entropy: PSF’s mean-plan documents are 11–13% shorter and switch topics more often. Its matched-entropy perplexity differences range from − 16 % -16\% to + 22 % +22\% across models and scoring windows, making them difficult to interpret as a plan effect alone. The mean plan also lowers MAUVE@512 from 0.86–0.88 to 0.71–0.75 and raises the lexical topic-switch rate from 11.8–13.7% to 30–47% (Appendix D.5 ). These summaries, and those in the code probe above, are interpolated to entropy 5.16. For PSF-L, MAUVE falls from 0.86–0.91 to 0.61–0.71 (read at entropy 5.18–5.26 without interpolation), and switch rates rise from 10% to 48–51% (real text: 3.6%). A fixed-setting check gives paired MAUVE scores of 0.866 versus 0.754 for sampled versus mean states (plain sampler, t = 0.75 t=0.75 , p = 0.95 p=0.95 , zero codes). MAUVE reflects a distributional change that includes sharing one plan across documents; lexical switches track within-document topic persistence. Finally, re-encoded outputs are closer to their own plan than another sample’s in 98% of documents: mean cosine is 0.40–0.41 versus 0.13–0.14 for blocks 2–8, except block 2 (0.11, as for a random plan). Sampled plans also cover encoded ones, with k k -nearest-neighbour precision 0.78–0.79 and recall 0.87–0.88 ( k = 5 k{=}5 ). Together, the probes support the plan’s role in organizing content.

sections.heading: Direct fine-tuning against the chain.
sections.text: Fine-tuning the pre-chain K = 64 K{=}64 block decoder directly at K = 8 K{=}8 with the last stage’s 6k steps reaches 24.5 against the chain’s 22.7 ± 0.4 22.7\pm 0.4 (three seeds). Continued to the chain’s total of 20k block-decoder steps, with its prior resumed for 30k more, it reaches 22.9 (chain 22.8), 21.6 at entropy 5.160 with nucleus 0.62 (chain 21.2) and a true-plan decode of 23.5 at 5.153 (chain 23.7 at 5.155). It loops slightly more (8.9% against 6.9% at t = 0.75 t{=}0.75 ). The initial gap therefore closes with additional decoder and prior training. The direct route’s 20k steps took 37 hours on eight H100s; we retain the chain, which spends fewer steps on expensive K = 8 K{=}8 rollouts and yields the K = 64 K{=}64 , 32 and 16 models as by-products.

sections.heading: Continued training of PSF-L.
sections.text: At K = 8 K{=}8 , continuing PSF-L’s block decoder for 6k and 12k more steps (+6% and +13% tokens) improves perplexity from 18.4 to 18.2 and 18.0 (seed sd 0.1), a modest gain over the tested extension. The K = 64 K{=}64 exception in Table 13 is more sensitive to training: PSF-L initially generates worse than PSF (42.2 against 39.2) despite better true-plan decode (35.1 against 40.3). Another 30k prior steps leave it at 42.6, while 10k more self-realized-prefix decoder steps and 30k prior steps bring it to 36.4 at entropy 5.16 (between 36.09 at 5.156 and 41.55 at 5.223), 7% ahead of PSF, with true-plan decode about 33.5 and looping at 8.3%. Its K = 64 K{=}64 stage had seen 22k self-realized-prefix steps at batch 192 against PSF’s 20k at batch 512. The improvement beyond prior-only continuation points to decoder adaptation as a contributing factor at this block length. The continued model is the star in Figure 4 ; Table 13 retains the original model for comparability along the chain.

sections.heading: B.4 Prior steps and refinement
sections.text: Changing the prior step count also shifts entropy at a fixed sampler setting, so we re-read the sweeps at entropy 5.16 with 32 and 64 instead of 50 steps. Every headline K = 8 K{=}8 value whose sweep brackets 5.16 changes by about 1%, with no consistent direction. For 50 → \to 32 / 64 steps, the readings are: plain 22.5 → \to 22.6 / 22.8 with the tightest pair (22.8 → \to 22.9 / 23.0 with the 0.70/0.80 pair of Appendix A.7 ); states-only nucleus 19.4 → \to 19.2 / 19.2, or 19.0 → \to 19.1 / 19.0 with the ban; PSF-L plain 18.4 → \to 18.3 / 18.5, and states-only with the ban 16.4 → \to 16.2 / 16.4. The re-read K = 8 K{=}8 ablations (Table 4 and Figure 3 (b)) move by at most 1.8%, except inference-time removal of the landing target at 64 steps ( + 2.9 % +2.9\% ). The shorter-block models are more sensitive. At K ≥ 16 K{\geq}16 , 32 steps cost 1–3.4% (PSF-L K = 32 K{=}32 : 6.5%), while 64 steps gain at most 1% (PSF-L K = 32 K{=}32 : 3.1%). Earlier runs with 20 and 12 steps gave + 0.3 % +0.3\% and − 0.2 % -0.2\% at K = 8 K{=}8 (nucleus 0.6), and + 2.4 % +2.4\% and + 5.2 % +5.2\% at K = 16 K{=}16 (guidance 4). A separate fixed-setting MAUVE@512 check gives 0.926 / 0.914 for the plain sampler and 0.847 / 0.834 for states-only with the ban, at 50 / 32 steps. It uses 1000 documents per setting and five quantization seeds on saved generations, rather than matched-entropy estimates. This check also finds small changes at K = 8 K{=}8 .

sections.heading: Runtime and comparison with ELF-B.
sections.text: At batch 32, the K = 8 K{=}8 plain sampler takes 25.9 / 27.2 / 28.2 ms per document at 32 / 50 / 64 steps in one session (Table 1 : 27.3 ms). Thus reducing prior steps gives a smaller reduction in end-to-end time. At 32 steps and entropy 5.16, PSF has lower perplexity than ELF-B (22.9 versus 24.0 with the 0.70/0.80 pair, 22.6 with the tightest; states-only 19.2 and 19.1), while ELF-B is faster at batch 32 (20.9 versus 25.9 ms). At 64 steps, PSF is faster (28.2 versus 40.9 ms); read at ELF-B’s entropy of 5.096, its plain sampler is close (19.6 versus 19.42) and the states-only rows have about 15% lower perplexity. We retain 50 steps as a common setting for our models in all tables.

sections.heading: Refinement.
sections.text: The optional refinement round of Section 2.5 rewrites every block; the reference setting uses guidance 1, nucleus 0.95 and temperature 0.8 in both passes. Sweeping both temperatures to compare at matched entropy, one round is 4–10% worse at every block length and size (PSF K = 8 K{=}8 , plain, 0.80 / 0.80: 22.8 at entropy 5.137 against 21.3 one-shot), and two rounds are 15% worse. At a fixed temperature, refinement also raises looping (10% to 15% at t = 0.70 t{=}0.70 , 4.3% to 6.5% at t = 0.80 t{=}0.80 ). Confidence-ordered partial commit, accepting half the blocks per round, brings perplexity within ± 2.5 % \pm 2.5\% of one-shot. These tested refinement settings provide no consistent improvement, so we use one-shot generation.

sections.heading: Throughput and batch size.
sections.text: Lower FLOPs coexist with greater serial depth: at K = 8 K{=}8 , PSF uses 0.31 TFLOPs and 178 dependent network evaluations, versus 7.2 TFLOPs and 33 for 32-step ELF-B (Table 14 ). At batch 1, ELF-B’s 0.13 s is faster than every PSF row (0.14–0.59 s). At batch 32, PSF with K ≥ 16 K\geq 16 reaches 60.4–70.2 documents per second against ELF-B’s 47.8 (1.26 × \times at K = 16 K{=}16 ), but K = 8 K{=}8 remains slower: 36.7 with plain sampling and 30.8 with the states-only sampler of Table 1 . Larger batches change the comparison. ELF-B moves only from 47.8 to 49.8 documents per second between batch 32 and 256, showing limited further batching benefit in this implementation. At batch 256, PSF reaches 62.9 with plain K = 8 K{=}8 (1.26 × \times ELF-B) and 93.7 with K = 16 K{=}16 (1.88 × \times ). The evaluated states-only K = 8 K{=}8 sampler is instead near parity (48.9 against 49.8, 0.98 × \times ). Thus the throughput advantage depends on both batch size and the sampler attached to the quality result.

sections.heading: Sampler overhead.
sections.text: The evaluated samplers cost more than greedy decoding: at K = 8 K{=}8 , + 2 +2 – 9 % 9\% at batch 1, + 2 % +2\% for temperature to + 22 % +22\% for nucleus with the ban at batch 32, and + 3.5 % +3.5\% to + 33 % +33\% at batch 256, mostly for the nucleus sort over the vocabulary. This token-selection overhead is separate from the prior: the states-only prior retains the same architecture and its sampling time agrees within 5% with the prior it replaces.

sections.heading: Autoregressive and other references.
sections.text: With CUDA graphs on both, the states-only K = 8 K{=}8 sampler of Table 1 is 6.5 × \times , 6.7 × \times and 6.6 × \times faster per document than the same-data AR at batch 1, 32 and 256. The AR takes 2927, 219.2 and 135.1 ms respectively (eager on the same machine: 8141 ms at batch 1 and 300.4 ms at batch 32). Against GPT-2 small, batch-32 speedups range from 4.0 × \times for states-only K = 8 K{=}8 to 9.0 × \times for K = 32 K{=}32 . PSF-L’s states-only K = 8 K{=}8 sampler reaches 22.2 documents per second at batch 32, 1.8 × \times ELF-M and 7.9 × \times ELF-L at 32 steps. BD3-LM and MDLM have no CUDA-graph sampler; their wall-clock entries describe the available eager implementations. FLOPs describe computation with less dependence on these implementation differences.

sections.heading: Appendix D Additional evaluations
sections.text: We first test how the perplexity comparisons depend on the judge, entropy anchor and document length. We then examine distributional similarity, diversity, repetition and lexical persistence, before evaluating coherence and prompted continuation. These checks establish the scope of the perplexity results and the document-quality limitations summarized in Section 5 . Unless otherwise specified, evaluations use 1000 documents and GPT-2 Large; each table specifies whether scores are measured or entropy-matched.

sections.heading: D.1 Other judges and other anchor entropies
sections.text: Changing the judge preserves the ordering of the K ≤ 16 K\leq 16 rows relative to the diffusion baselines in Table 15 . We re-scored the evaluation dumps of Table 1 , its sweeps and every baseline with Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B, using each judge’s own tokens for both perplexity and per-document entropy. These judges differ from GPT-2 in model family, training corpus and tokenizer. The dumps are unchanged except for the same-data AR, re-sampled at nucleus 0.86–0.88 to bracket entropy 5.16. ELF-B’s 32-step entropy is 5.158 in GPT-2 tokens and 5.159 in Qwen tokens, allowing the same rounded anchor within each judge’s protocol. The broader ordering is more stable than the close comparisons. The plain K = 8 K{=}8 margin over ELF-B shrinks from about 5 % 5\% to 3 % 3\% , while PSF-L’s states-only rows move ahead of the same-data AR under both Qwen judges and K = 64 K{=}64 falls behind BD3-LM block 4. GPT-2 small retains its low perplexity under Qwen as well; its measured entropy is marked where it differs from 5.16. Table 15 retains the full scores and these exceptions. The entropy sweep identifies a separate limit: the advantage over ELF-M and ELF-L is specific to the 5.0–5.2 nat band. sections.heading: D.2 Document length, MAUVE and a length-controlled window
sections.text: Document length matters because per-document entropy grows with length: shorter outputs start lower on the entropy axis and are moved further up their perplexity–entropy curve when matched to 5.16. Although the canvas is fixed at L = 1024 L=1024 , scoring stops at the first end-of-text token. Held-out documents average 956 T5 tokens and 65% end before the canvas; ours average 959–979 tokens. ELF-B and ELF-M usually fill the canvas (1016–1018 tokens, 98–99% at the canvas), whereas BD3-LM and MDLM are shorter (means 752 and 733; medians 872 and 828, against 985 for held-out text). We therefore evaluate a common 512-judge-token window for both re-scoring and MAUVE; Cosmos uses a separate MAUVE@256 protocol (Appendix A.4 ). The window check preserves the comparison with ELF-B and substantially narrows the gap to BD3-LM. Table 15 re-scores both perplexity and entropy on the first 512 GPT-2 Large tokens and re-matches at ELF-B’s 32-step window entropy, 4.845. The plain K = 8 K{=}8 and states-only samplers are respectively 21 % 21\% and 34 % 34\% ahead of ELF-B (20.4 and 17.0–17.1 against 25.8). Their advantage over BD3-LM block 4 falls from roughly a factor of two to 7–23%: its window score is 22.0, bracketed by fresh samplings at nucleus 0.80 and 0.85. The same-data AR and GPT-2 small remain ahead (15.0 and 12.7). This all-documents window includes outputs shorter than 512 tokens; restricting to longer documents moves our rows by at most 0.2 but retains only 68% of BD3-LM’s documents. Thus part of the original BD3-LM gap comes from the length protocol. MAUVE reveals a distributional cost of the lowest-perplexity settings. At K ≤ 16 K\leq 16 , the plain samplers score 0.90–0.93, numerically matching or exceeding every evaluated diffusion baseline and GPT-2 small, while the same-data AR reaches 0.93–0.95. The states-only scores fall to 0.85–0.89 for PSF and 0.88–0.91 for PSF-L, compared with 0.90–0.93 for their plain samplers. These ranges are above ELF-B at 32 steps (0.73), around its 64-step score (0.89), and below the same-data AR; plain K = 64 K{=}64 is also lower at 0.87. The standard deviation over five quantization seeds is 0.003–0.037. MAUVE measures similarity to the held-out distribution in the judge’s feature space (Appendix A.3 ); the decrease motivates the diversity checks below, while document coherence is evaluated separately.

sections.heading: D.3 Diversity and overlap with the training set
sections.text: Per-document entropy can remain high even when generated documents resemble one another. Table 16 therefore measures diversity across the dump: Distinct-4 is the fraction of distinct T5-token 4-grams, and Self-BLEU-4 , computed on lowercased words, scores each of 300 documents against the other 299 (higher means more resemblance). Every generator is less diverse than real text by these measures. Our plain rows resemble ELF-B (Self-BLEU 0.301 and 0.296 against 0.292), while the states-only operating points are less diverse (0.36–0.40, with distinct-4 0.74–0.75); all our rows have higher Self-BLEU than the same-data AR (0.23). The lower-perplexity configurations thus also concentrate the generated document distribution. Verbatim training overlap addresses a different question. We index 13-grams from the first 1024 T5 tokens of two million training documents (1.9B tokens), then measure the fraction of each evaluation dump’s 13-grams found in the index. Held-out documents were never indexed and provide a reference for overlap within OpenWebText. The states-only rows share 0.5–1.0% of their 13-grams with the index, below GPT-2 small’s 1.4%; autoregressive decoders generally overlap more than token-level diffusion models (0.4–1.4% against 0.04–0.15%), with PSF-L highest among ours. All measured overlap rates remain below held-out text (2.7%). This statistic measures overlap with the indexed training subset, including shared quotations and boilerplate; it is not a measure of text quality. A separate position check finds no late increase in judge negative log-likelihood: after pooling tokens into 128-token bins, the ratio of the second half to the second bin is 0.82–0.91 for our models, against 0.85 for held-out text and 0.90 for ELF-B. This local predictability diagnostic leaves open whether the document remains coherent, which we examine in Appendix D.6 . sections.heading: D.5 Topic persistence and lexical coupling
sections.text: Lower perplexity in the states-only configurations is accompanied by weaker lexical persistence across chunks. Each block samples its realization of the shared plan, with limited coupling through the landing target. Figure 11 shows the resulting lexical continuity: our one-shot nucleus sample has J 1 = 8.0 J_{1}=8.0 and a switch rate of 6.8%, while the states-only rows have J 1 = 4.3 J_{1}=4.3 –5.8 and switch rates of 10–14%. Real OpenWebText, ELF-B and GPT-2 small have higher overlap ( J 1 J_{1} 13–16) and fewer switches (1.5–3.6%). BD3-LM illustrates that the two measures need not rank systems identically: its J 1 J_{1} is lower at 10.7 but its switch rate is only 0.8%. For these measures, we split documents into consecutive chunks of 45 content words after removing stop words, punctuation and numbers. J 1 J_{1} is the mean Jaccard overlap of adjacent chunks’ word sets divided by the mean overlap between chunks from different documents; the switch rate counts adjacent pairs within 1.5 times this cross-document floor. To test whether directly sharing lexical choices helps, we add a sampling-time bonus: after the nucleus cut, tokens with T5 identifiers ≥ 2000 \geq 2000 that another block has emitted receive logit bonus b b . This token-ID rule is a heuristic for selecting content tokens. With b = 3 b=3 , the code-augmented K = 8 K=8 model reaches J 1 = 15.6 ± 0.4 J_{1}=15.6\pm 0.4 and a 1.6% switch rate over three seeds, at perplexity 23.89 ± 0.27 23.89\pm 0.27 and entropy 5.155. sections.heading: D.6 LLM-judged coherence
sections.text: The perplexity margins do not carry over to the coherence judgements tested here. We use two instruction-tuned judges in blinded pairwise comparisons, drawing 200 seeded document pairs for each system pair and presenting each in both orders. Only pairs whose preferred passage is unchanged by the order count as consistent. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (bf16, greedy) reads the first 300 words and judges internal coherence (one topic, consistent facts, no contradictions) and resemblance to a single human-written article. Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct judges coherence on words 1–300, words 300–600 (past the first two or three block seams), and the whole document. The real-against-real row calibrates the 7B judge, which has a strong slot preference. Both judges strongly prefer real text to every generator they evaluate (Table 18 ). sections.heading: D.7 Prompted continuation without retraining
sections.text: Predictive states allow prompted continuation through plan inpainting without retraining for this task. Given the first P = 256 P=256 tokens of a held-out document ( m = P / ℓ m=P/\ell blocks), the encoder yields the exact states 𝒔 1 , … , 𝒔 m + 1 {\bm{s}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{s}}_{m+1} and codes 𝒓 1 , … , 𝒓 m {\bm{r}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{r}}_{m} . The prior fills the remaining plan by replacement inpainting: at every Euler step, the given entries are reset to their exact noisy value, RePaint-style, optionally with r r resampling passes per step. All blocks then decode in parallel, with prompt blocks forced to the given tokens. We evaluate 500 held-out documents with at least 512 tokens, measuring continuation perplexity under GPT-2 Large given the prompt, per-document entropy, and prompt relevance . Relevance is the fraction of continuation content words (alphabetic, at least four letters, not a stop word) occurring in the prompt, minus the fraction for mismatched prompt–continuation pairs (chance, about 2%). GPT-2 small and the same-data AR continue the same prompts. The “oracle plan” uses the encoder’s plan of the full real document with only the prompt blocks forced, providing a decoder reference with the prior bypassed. Inpainting alone gives weak lexical relevance: 0.7% above chance with the plain sampler. Combining r = 4 r=4 resampling passes and lexical coupling b = 3 b=3 raises it to 4.4–5.2%, compared with 6.8% for real continuations and 6.5% for the same-data AR (Figure 12 ). The score reaches the range of the measured oracle-plan rows (4.5–4.7%), but those rows use different samplers and entropies, so they do not establish an upper bound on prompt use. Perplexities span 14.6–23.4, against 15.1 for GPT-2 small and 17.7 for the same-data AR, also at different entropies. GPT-2 small’s overlap exceeds that of real continuations, illustrating that lexical reuse alone does not establish continuation quality.

sections.heading: A separately fine-tuned prompt-attention path.
sections.text: To test direct access to prompt tokens, we add a third sub-layer per block that cross-attends to them (19M parameters) and fine-tune for 6k steps. Unconditional perplexity remains similar (22.4 at entropy 5.16), while raw prompt overlap is 3.2% against 3.0% with the prompt withheld. Under teacher forcing with true predictive states, the extra prompt tokens lower continuation negative log-likelihood by only 0.2%, suggesting little training incentive to use this path in that setup. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.12898v1 [cs.CL] 09 Oct 2026 Rethinking the Roles of Diffusion and Decoding: Predictive-State Flows for Parallel Language Generation Jinjin He Email: jhe433@gatech.edu Xinsong Feng Email: xsfeng@gatech.edu Lucheng Fu Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: luchengfu@gatech.edu Sinan Wang Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: swang3081@gatech.edu Bo Zhu Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: bo.zhu@gatech.edu Jiayun Wang Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: pjwang@gatech.edu Abstract In continuous diffusion language models (DLMs), latents generated by the diffusion prior are mapped almost deterministically to tokens, either by a decoder or through a token embedding matrix. Unlike in image generation, where visual details can vary continuously, the diffusion prior must capture fine-grained discrete token choices in continuous space, which can make the joint latent distribution difficult to model. We argue that generative roles should instead be divided: the diffusion prior should generate high-level predictive information , while the decoder should resolve the remaining token-level choices. Based on this view, we introduce Predictive-State Flows (PSF), which partitions a sequence into blocks and associates each block with a predictive state computed solely from the preceding context. A rectified-flow prior generates the sequence of predictive states, after which a block-causal decoder generates all blocks in parallel, autoregressively only within each block. This design reduces diffusion from L L token-level states to K ≪ L K\ll L predictive states and reduces token-level sequential depth to L / K L/K . On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter model with K = 8 K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 using 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token document, compared with 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B with 32 sampling steps. The corresponding measured operating points yield MAUVE@512 of 0.93 and 0.73, respectively. Controlled comparisons further show that content states, which additionally encode their own blocks, yield 8–16% higher generative perplexity than predictive states, and that replacing sampled predictive-state trajectories with a shared mean lowers MAUVE@512 by 0.11. These results suggest that latent design for continuous DLMs should consider not only how compactly text is represented, but also how generative roles are divided between the prior and the decoder. 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 Introduction Diffusion language models (DLMs) generate text by iteratively refining multiple token positions in parallel rather than decoding strictly from left to right ( Li et al., 2022 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Nie et al., 2026 ) . Continuous DLMs perform this refinement over continuous states that are subsequently decoded into text ( Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ; Hu et al., 2026 ) . In many existing formulations, the generated states are mapped nearly deterministically to tokens ( Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Hu et al., 2024 ) . This assigns most generative roles to the diffusion prior: it must specify fine-grained token choices, while the decoder largely recovers choices already encoded in those states. This raises a fundamental question: which information should be generated by the diffusion prior, and which decisions should be left to the decoder? This division of roles arises in part from how continuous text representations are commonly learned. An encoder maps an observed token sequence to latents, and a decoder is trained to reconstruct the same sequence ( Lovelace et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Such an objective encourages the latents to preserve the specific token choices that distinguish the observed text from other plausible realizations, leaving the prior responsible for generating those choices. Unlike in image generation, where perceptual compression can discard visually negligible details and represent the remaining variation continuously ( Rombach et al., 2022 ; Esser et al., 2024 ) , reconstruction-based text latents tend to preserve fine-grained discrete token distinctions. The diffusion prior must therefore model these distinctions and their dependencies in continuous space, making the joint latent distribution difficult to learn. We therefore propose a different division of generative roles: the diffusion prior generates predictive information that guides subsequent content, while a decoder resolves the remaining local token choices. We instantiate this principle using predictive states . Given a sequence x 1 : L ∈ 𝒱 L x_{1:L}\in\mathcal{V}^{L} divided into K K consecutive blocks, we associate each block k k with a continuous state 𝒔 k = E ψ ​ ( x ( < k ) ) , {\bm{s}}_{k}=E_{\psi}\left(x^{(<k)}\right), (1) which summarizes the context preceding block k k without observing the block itself. The state therefore provides information for predicting the upcoming block, rather than directly encoding its specific token choices. We use a rectified-flow prior ( Liu et al., 2022 ) to generate the predictive-state trajectory 𝒔 1 : K {\bm{s}}_{1:K} . Conditioned on these states, a block-causal decoder predicts all K K blocks in parallel, with autoregressive decoding restricted to within each block. We call the resulting framework Predictive-State Flow (PSF). However, this division of roles introduces a consistency challenge. Because the full predictive-state trajectory is generated before token decoding, independently decoded blocks may become inconsistent at their boundaries. We coordinate adjacent blocks through a one-token landing target : after the first parallel decoding step, block k k can condition on the first generated token of block k + 1 k+1 , providing a lightweight constraint on their transition. We further adapt the decoder to rollout states produced by the learned prior, reducing the train–generation mismatch. This division also supports parallel generation: the prior operates on K ≪ L K\ll L predictive states, while the decoder generates the corresponding blocks concurrently. With autoregression restricted to within each block, the decoder requires only L / K L/K sequential token-generation steps instead of L L . Our experiments directly evaluate this division of generative roles. On unconditional OpenWebText generation, a 197M-parameter PSF model with K = 8 K=8 achieves a generative perplexity of 22.8 at entropy 5.16 while requiring only 0.31 TFLOPs per 1024-token sequence, compared with 24.0 and 7.2 TFLOPs for ELF-B. In a controlled comparison, content states that also encode their own block are 8–16% worse than predictive states. Under nucleus sampling, PSF achieves a generative perplexity of 19.4 when the prior generates only predictive states, compared with 21.2 when it additionally generates latent variables carrying information about each block’s token realization. This supports leaving local token choices to the decoder at long block lengths. Further reducing K K from 64 to 8 also improves perplexity from 39.2 to 22.8 while lowering the computational cost of the diffusion prior. This reflect a trade-off between the latent-generation difficulty and the amount of local autoregressive realization. Same-hardware measurements further show that lower FLOPs do not translate directly into wall-clock speedups, as latency and throughput vary with both block length and batch size. Our contributions are summarized as follows. First, we introduce predictive states , which allow the diffusion prior to model high-level predictive information while leaving token-level realization to the decoder. Second, we develop PSF, which generates a short predictive-state trajectory with rectified flow and decodes the corresponding blocks in parallel, using one-token landing targets to coordinate adjacent blocks and local autoregression within each block to limit sequential decoding depth. Third, we empirically study this division of generative roles, showing that predictive states outperform content states and that strong generation quality at long block lengths can be achieved without requiring the prior to encode block-specific token information. 2 Predictive-State Flow We begin by separating the generation of predictive information from token-level realization. PSF uses a rectified-flow prior to generate a trajectory of predictive states , while a predictive block decoder generates the corresponding token-level realizations. Each predictive state summarizes the context preceding a block without encoding the block itself, allowing the prior to model predictive information while leaving local token choices to the block decoder. The block decoder realizes all blocks in parallel, while a one-token landing target couples adjacent branches to improve consistency across block boundaries. 2.1 Predictive States We divide a sequence x 1 : L ∈ 𝒱 L x_{1:L}\in\mathcal{V}^{L} into K K consecutive blocks x ( 1 ) , … , x ( K ) x^{(1)},\dots,x^{(K)} of length ℓ = L / K \ell=L/K and associate each block k k with a predictive state 𝒔 k ∈ ℝ d {\bm{s}}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that summarizes the context preceding that block. To ensure that each state contains only information available from the corresponding prefix, we use a block-causal encoder in which representations in block j j depend only on tokens in blocks 1 , … , j 1,\dots,j . We mean-pool the outputs of block j j to obtain a context state 𝒄 j = f ψ ​ ( x ( ≤ j ) ) . {\bm{c}}_{j}=f_{\psi}\!\left(x^{(\leq j)}\right). By construction, 𝒔 k {\bm{s}}_{k} depends only on x ( < k ) x^{(<k)} , unlike content latents that encode a particular realization of their own block ( Lovelace et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . We refer to the predictive-state trajectory 𝐒 = ( 𝒔 1 , … , 𝒔 K ) \mathbf{S}=({\bm{s}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{s}}_{K}) , optionally together with the realization codes introduced in Section 2.4 , as the document plan . The diffusion prior models this plan, while the block decoder resolves the token-level realization of each block. 2.2 Parallel Block Decoder with Landing Targets Given the predictive states, the block decoder generates the K K blocks in parallel, with causal self-attention within each block. Block k k cross-attends to 𝒔 ≤ k {\bm{s}}_{\leq k} under a causal mask over the block index. Because predictive states do not specify a unique local realization, independently generated blocks can each be plausible while remaining inconsistent across block boundaries. We address this issue with a one-token landing target . The first decoding step generates the first token of every block in parallel. From the second step onward, block k k additionally conditions on the first token of block k + 1 k+1 . During training, this target is the ground-truth token, whereas during generation it is the token produced at the first decoding step. Let τ k = x 1 ( k + 1 ) \tau_{k}=x^{(k+1)}_{1} for k < K k<K , and let τ K \tau_{K} denote the learned “no-target” embedding supplied to the final block. The decoder therefore requires only ℓ \ell sequential token-generation steps, rather than L L for standard autoregressive decoding. 2.3 Flow Prior over Predictive States We model the joint distribution of predictive-state trajectories with a rectified-flow prior ( Liu et al., 2022 ; Lipman et al., 2022 ) . After training the encoder and decoder, we freeze both and use the encoder to map each training sequence to a trajectory 𝐒 = ( 𝒔 1 , … , 𝒔 K ) \mathbf{S}=({\bm{s}}_{1},\dots,{\bm{s}}_{K}) . We first jointly train the encoder and block decoder for reconstruction. We then freeze the encoder trunk and fine-tune the decoder to improve robustness to generated predictive states, introduce block-specific realization codes, and adapt the model across different block lengths. Finally, we freeze the encoder and decoder and train the flow prior over the resulting plans. Model-specific training schedules and hyperparameters are provided in Appendix A.2 . Stage I: reconstruction training. We first jointly train the encoder and block decoder using token-level cross-entropy, adding Gaussian noise to the predictive states read by the decoder. For block k k , the decoder conditions on the predictive states 𝒔 ≤ k {\bm{s}}_{\leq k} , which summarize only the preceding blocks. Stage II: decoder fine-tuning. We next freeze the encoder trunk and further train the block decoder in three steps: adapting it to rollout states, introducing block-specific realization codes, and adapting it across different block lengths. Training on generated states. During initial training, the block decoder conditions on predictive states encoded from ground-truth sequences. At generation time, however, it conditions on states produced by the flow prior rather than states directly encoded from ground-truth text. To reduce this mismatch, we generate a no-gradient rollout conditioned on the ground-truth predictive states and re-encode the resulting sequence. For each block independently, we replace the original predictive state with its re-encoded counterpart with probability 0.5 0.5 , while keeping the original token targets unchanged. The rollout uses temperature 0.65 0.65 and nucleus sampling with p = 0.95 p=0.95 . We provide a binary source label λ k \lambda_{k} for each predictive state, where λ k = 1 \lambda_{k}=1 denotes an original encoder state and λ k = 0 \lambda_{k}=0 denotes a rollout state. A zero-initialized embedding of λ k \lambda_{k} is added to 𝒔 k {\bm{s}}_{k} . At generation time, we set λ k = 0 \lambda_{k}=0 for all blocks. Realization codes. The predictive state 𝒔 k = 𝒄 k − 1 {\bm{s}}_{k}={\bm{c}}_{k-1} is computed before block k k is observed and therefore contains only information from the preceding blocks. We next augment the decoder with a low-dimensional realization code 𝒓 k ∈ ℝ 64 {\bm{r}}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{64} from the unshifted encoder state 𝒄 k = f ψ ​ ( x ( ≤ k ) ) {\bm{c}}_{k}=f_{\psi}(x^{(\leq k)}) , which additionally contains information from block k k . A newly added linear head predicts the mean and diagonal variance of a Gaussian posterior, q ψ ​ ( 𝒓 k ∣ 𝒄 k ) = 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝝁 ψ ​ ( 𝒄 k ) , diag ⁡ ( 𝝈 ψ 2 ​ ( 𝒄 k ) ) ) . q_{\psi}({\bm{r}}_{k}\mid{\bm{c}}_{k})=\mathcal{N}\!\left({\bm{\mu}}_{\psi}({\bm{c}}_{k}),\operatorname{diag}\!\left(\bm{\sigma}_{\psi}^{2}({\bm{c}}_{k})\right)\right). (7) The block decoder conditions on both 𝒓 k {\bm{r}}_{k} and the next-block code 𝒓 k + 1 {\bm{r}}_{k+1} , sampled from their posteriors during training. During this stage, the encoder trunk remains frozen, while the decoder, code head, and newly introduced code-conditioning layers are trained jointly. We regularize the posterior toward 𝒩 ⁡ ( 𝟎 , 𝑰 ) \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},{\bm{I}}) with a KL budget of ℓ \ell nats per block that limits the amount of block-specific information carried by 𝒓 k {\bm{r}}_{k} . Further details of the posterior and conditioning architecture are provided in Appendix A.2 . Training across block lengths. Starting from K = 64 K=64 , we successively fine-tune the decoder at K = 32 K=32 , 16 16 , and 8 8 , while keeping the encoder trunk frozen. Stage III: flow-prior training. Finally, we freeze the encoder and block decoder and train the flow prior described in Section 2.3 . For each training sequence, we encode the predictive states 𝒔 k {\bm{s}}_{k} and use the posterior mean 𝝁 k {\bm{\mu}}_{k} as the target realization code. The prior is trained to jointly generate these representations using the flow-matching objective defined in the previous section. We train a separate prior for each value of K K , warm-started from the previous block length. For K = 8 K=8 , we additionally train a states-only prior that generates only the predictive states, using zero code targets. We retain the code-trained block decoder and fix all its realization-code inputs to 𝟎 \mathbf{0} . At inference time, we use generated codes for K ≥ 16 K\geq 16 and the states-only prior for K = 8 K=8 (Section 3.4 ). 2.5 Generation and Refinement For generation, we first sample the predictive-state trajectory from the flow prior, together with realization codes when they are used. The block decoder then generates all K K blocks in parallel over ℓ = L / K \ell=L/K autoregressive steps. The first decoding step produces the landing targets, after which each branch conditions on the first token of the following block and continues independently. We set λ k = 0 \lambda_{k}=0 for all blocks during generation. The resulting serial depth is 50 + ℓ 50+\ell , compared with L L steps for standard autoregressive generation. Optionally, we refine the generated document by re-encoding it and running the block decoder again. When realization codes are used, they are recomputed from the re-encoded sequence. Because refinement conditions on encoder-produced states, we set λ k = 1 \lambda_{k}=1 . Each refinement round requires one encoder pass followed by another ℓ \ell -step parallel decode. 3 Experiments Dataset and evaluation.
