Discrete DLMs corrupt tokens with multinomial or masking noise and learn to reverse it ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Lou et al., 2023 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ) ; continuous DLMs embed tokens and denoise the embeddings ( Li et al., 2022 ; Gulrajani and Hashimoto, 2023 ) . ELF ( Hu et al., 2026 ) keeps the sequence in a frozen T5 embedding space and reaches a generative perplexity of 24 on OpenWebText in 32 steps; our prior borrows its self-conditioning ( Chen et al., 2022 ) and guidance-scale tokens ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . All of these models denoise the full L L -token sequence at every step; our prior denoises K ≪ L K\ll L latents, and tokens are produced by a separate block decoder. Block-wise and semi-autoregressive generation. BD3-LM ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) , SSD-LM ( Han et al., 2023 ) and AR-Diffusion ( Wu et al., 2023 ) are autoregressive across blocks and diffuse within each block; BD3-LM’s quality degrades as the block grows (Section 3.3 ). Our model is the transpose—diffusion across blocks, autoregression within—so the two families live on one axis, the block length, and we report both ends of it under one ruler. Blockwise parallel, multi-head and speculative decoding ( Stern et al., 2018 ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Leviathan et al., 2023 ) propose tokens and verify them with an autoregressive model; our blocks need no verification step: there is no separate target model to match, and the plan and the landing token are the only cross-block inputs. Planning and hierarchical generation. Plan-and-Write ( Yao et al., 2019 ) uses explicit keyword storylines to guide story generation, while Skeleton-of-Thought ( Ning et al., 2024 ) expands a prompted textual outline in parallel. The Latent Transformer ( Kaiser et al., 2018 ) autoregressively generates a shorter sequence of discrete latents and decodes the target translation in parallel. Our flow prior generates continuous predictive states jointly, and the block decoder realizes tokens autoregressively within each block. Latent diffusion for text. LD4LG ( Lovelace et al., 2023 ) and PLANNER ( Zhang et al., 2023 ) run diffusion in a learned latent space of a sentence or paragraph and decode it autoregressively; Large Concept Models ( Barrault et al., 2024 ) generate sentence embeddings and decode each into its sentence. These representations encode the content to be generated. We generate a sequence of predictive states that exclude their own block, predict the blocks in parallel , and couple adjacent blocks with a one-token landing target. 5 Conclusion This work revisits what a diffusion prior should generate in a continuous diffusion language model. Rather than requiring continuous states to specify the final token sequence, PSF assigns different generative roles to the prior and the decoder: the flow prior generates a short trajectory of predictive states that describe what should come next, while a block decoder resolves the corresponding token-level realizations. One-token landing targets provide lightweight coupling between blocks while preserving parallel block generation. This division of roles yields both computational and modeling benefits. With only K = 8 K=8 predictive states for a 1024-token document, PSF uses 23 × \times fewer FLOPs than 32-step ELF-B while achieving lower generative perplexity, higher MAUVE, and higher batched throughput. When the prior generates predictive states alone, nucleus sampling further reduces matched-entropy perplexity to approximately 20% below ELF-B. More importantly, predictive states consistently outperform content states that additionally encode their own blocks, and increasing block length improves PSF even as it degrades block diffusion. Together, these results suggest that continuous language-model latents should be designed not only for what they represent, but also for how generative roles are divided between the prior and the decoder. A useful latent need not preserve every detail of the output; it can instead represent information that is easy for a continuous prior to generate and sufficient for a decoder to turn into coherent text. Predictive states provide one realization of this principle, and point toward continuous generative models in which priors and decoders are designed jointly around the information each is best suited to generate. Limitations and future work. Our main limitation is scale: all experiments use at most 677M generation parameters, a fixed 1024-token canvas and unconditional OpenWebText generation; larger models and longer sequences remain unexplored. Blocks are decoded in parallel from a shared plan, coupled only by one-token landing targets, so whether many blocks stay consistent in topic, entities and discourse over longer documents is untested; topic persistence is already the weakest aspect of our samples (Appendix D.5 ). The most pressing next steps are to scale model size and sequence length, to couple blocks more strongly than through a single token, and to measure long-range coherence, which generative perplexity misses. Prompted continuation works without retraining but uses the prompt weakly, calling for a prompt-conditioned prior. Autoregressive models remain ahead, although the gap to the same-data baseline narrows at our largest scale (Appendix A.6 ), and the states-only configuration trades topic persistence, diversity and judged coherence for lower perplexity. The FLOP saving over ELF becomes a throughput advantage only at large batch, and the training recipe has several stages, including realization codes whose benefit we only partly understand; faster small-batch sampling and a simpler recipe remain future work.
